title: Count the lakes
statement:
A satellite map is a grid where 1 is water and 0 is land. A lake is a group of water cells connected up, down, left or right (not diagonally).

Given the grid `grid`, return how many lakes there are.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Do diagonal cells connect?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: No, only up, down, left and right.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Can the grid be empty or have rows of different lengths?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: It can be empty; all rows have the same length.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Can I modify the grid?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Prefer not to; use a visited set.
clarifyingQuestions.why: Avoids side effects on the input.

clarifyingQuestions.question: How big can the grid be?
clarifyingQuestions.why: Deep recursion could overflow; an explicit stack is safer.

edgeCases.why: One lake even though it surrounds land.

approaches.name: Flood fill with DFS or BFS
approaches.idea: Scan every cell. When you find unvisited water, count a new lake and mark every connected water cell visited.
approaches.tradeoffs: Standard; each cell is visited once.

approaches.name: Union-find
approaches.idea: Union each water cell with water neighbors, then count distinct roots.
approaches.tradeoffs: Useful when cells are added over time; more code here.

optimal.name: Flood fill
optimal.explanation: Loop over cells. On an unvisited water cell, increment the count and explore its lake with an explicit stack (or queue), marking cells visited when pushed and pushing in-bounds water neighbors in four directions.

hintLadder: When you find a water cell, how would you find the rest of its lake?
How do you make sure you don’t count the same lake twice?
This is a graph where cells are nodes. Which traversals do you know?
Scan the grid; on unvisited water, count it and flood-fill its lake with DFS or BFS.

expectedMentions.what: Describes the grid as a graph of cells
Proposes flood fill with DFS or BFS and O(rows * cols) time
Explains marking cells visited to avoid recounting
Mentions recursion depth or uses an explicit stack

followUps: Return the size of the largest lake.
Cells turn into water one at a time; report the lake count after each change.

walkthrough.say: Only up, down, left and right connect, not diagonals? And should I avoid changing the grid?

Each lake is a connected component of water cells. I’ll scan every cell; when I hit water I haven’t visited, that’s a new lake, and I flood-fill to mark the whole lake visited. Every cell is handled a constant number of times, so O(rows times cols).
A big lake could make recursion very deep, so I’ll use an explicit stack.
Outer scan; a new lake when I find unvisited water.
I mark cells when I push them, so nothing gets pushed twice.

In the example, the top-left 1 starts lake one and the fill reaches its right neighbor and the 1 below that. The 1 in row 1, column 3 starts lake two and reaches the one below it. The bottom-left 1 is lake three. Answer 3.
For the diagonal grid, the two ones don’t touch in four directions, so 2.
O(rows times cols) time and space.
